tasks.task: We're a 25-person EU SaaS (project management tool, controller for our own user accounts). On 3 March a user, Mariela Sousa (mariela.sousa@example.com, user ID 48213), emailed support@ asking 'for everything you hold on me' and also to delete her account afterwards. Support only forwarded it to me on 6 March. Please log the intake with the correct clock start date and deadline, flag the erasure request as a separate ticket, and propose a proportionate identity verification step since she wrote from the email on her account.
tasks.rationale: Follows the skill's output structure: all 8 sections in order, questions listed at the top, and [CONFIRM] placeholders instead of invented data. Clock start is correctly the day of receipt (3 March), not the 6 March forwarding date. The weekend and holiday rollover is handled conservatively with a verify note. Erasure is split into a separate ticket with its own clock, and deletion is held until access is delivered, with the requester told. Identity is Tier 1 with no passport request, a red-flag check, secure delivery, and an escalation path with the clock treated as running. The search plan, redaction log (colleague identities, hashes, internal opinions disclosed) and acknowledgement letter all match the skill. Escalation triggers are listed. It also usefully offers the marketing opt-out. Minor gaps: it assumed a year (flagged transparently) and anchored the year-assumption caveat for 2026 usefully. The 2027 date assumption is a small risk, but it is handled well.

# DSAR intake: Mariela Sousa (access + erasure)

**Questions before the next step:**
1. What year was the request received? I've assumed 2027 because the year wasn't stated. If it was 2026, see the note in section 3.
2. Is Mariela a member of any B2B customer's workspace? If so, you are likely processor for the project content there.
3. Has her account had any recent email change, password reset or new-device login? This affects the identity tier.
4. Please share your system inventory or RoPA and sub-processor list so the search plan can name real systems.

---

## 1. DSAR log entry

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| DSAR ID | `[CONFIRM: DSAR-2027-NNN]` |
| Linked ticket | Erasure (Art. 17), logged separately as `[CONFIRM: DSAR-2027-NNN+1]` |
| Received | **2027-03-03**, by email to support@ |
| Received by compliance | 2027-03-06, forwarded by support. This has **no effect on the clock.** |
| Requester | Mariela Sousa, mariela.sousa@example.com, user ID 48213 |
| Relationship | End user / account holder. Workspace memberships: `[CONFIRM]` |
| Representative | None, self-made request |
| Request wording | "everything you hold on me", then delete account afterwards |
| Rights requested | Access (Art. 15); erasure (Art. 17), split out |
| Role | Controller for her account data. Processor role for any customer-workspace content: `[CONFIRM]` |
| Identity | Tier 1: sent from registered account email (see section 4) |
| Statutory due date | 2027-04-03, which is a Saturday (see section 3) |
| Internal send-by target | **Fri 2027-04-02** |
| Extension | Not anticipated |
| Acknowledgement | To send today (see section 7) |
| Owner / approver | `[CONFIRM: compliance officer name]` / `[CONFIRM: DPO if appointed]` |

## 2. Scope and role decision

- **This is a valid DSAR.** "Everything you hold on me" sent to any company inbox is an Art. 15 request. No form or legal citation is needed.
- **Controller part:** account and profile, auth and login history, billing, support tickets, CRM and marketing records, product analytics, security and app logs, internal comms about her. Answer this part in full.
- **Possible processor part:** if she works in a workspace owned by a B2B customer, the project content there is processed on that customer's instructions.
  - Forward that part to the customer's admin under your DPA (Art. 28(3)(e)).
  - Tell her which organisation is the controller for it.
  - `[CONFIRM: workspace memberships and DPA terms]`
- **Bundled erasure request: flagged as a separate ticket, not processed here.**
  - It has its own one-month clock from **3 March**.
  - Hand it to whoever owns erasure.
  - **Hold the deletion until the access response is delivered.** Her data is in scope of the pending access request and must not be altered or deleted in the meantime.
  - Tell her you are doing this (wording is in the acknowledgement below).
  - When erasure is processed, retention obligations such as invoices under tax law will limit what can be deleted. That is for the erasure ticket.

## 3. Deadline

- **Clock start: 3 March 2027.** That is the day the request reached the company, at support@. The 3-day internal forwarding delay does not move the start date.
- **Calendar-month rule:** due on the same date in the following month, **3 April 2027**.
- **Weekend issue:** 3 April 2027 is a **Saturday**.
  - Under Reg. 1182/71, which the EDPB Guidelines 01/2022 refer to, a period ending on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday may roll to the next working day (Mon 5 April).
  - Do not rely on that. Verify with your supervisory authority's practice and plan to send by **Friday 2 April**.
- **If the year was 2026:** 3 April 2026 is **Good Friday**, a public holiday in many member states. The same conservative approach applies: aim to send by Thu 2 April 2026.
- **Internal milestones (2027):**

| Milestone | Date |
|---|---|
| Processor and vendor responses due (T-14) | 19 Mar |
| Draft complete (T-7) | 26 Mar |
| Sign-off (T-3) | 31 Mar |
| Send | 2 Apr |

- **Extension (Art. 12(3)):** not justified on current facts. One user of a 25-person SaaS is not unusually complex.
  - If one becomes necessary, the notice with reasons must reach her **before 3 April**.
  - Staff holiday or backlog are not valid reasons.
- **Process lesson:** the 3 days lost at support are a common weakness. Consider a short briefing for support: forward any "my data" request to compliance the same day.

## 4. Identity decision

- **Tier 1 (low).** The request came from mariela.sousa@example.com, the email registered on account 48213. Under Art. 12(6), more information may only be requested where there are *reasonable doubts*. A matching registered email is normally enough.
- **Do not ask for a passport or ID copy.** That would be disproportionate and would collect data you do not need.
- **Proportionate steps instead:**
  1. **Red-flag check (internal, no contact needed).** Look for these in the last ~30 days:
     - a change of account email
     - a password reset
     - new-device or unusual-location logins
     - a request to deliver to a different address

     If none, record "Verified Tier 1 on [date]: request from registered email, no red flags."
  2. **Secure delivery as a built-in safeguard.** Deliver the export only to the registered email via an expiring link, ideally into an authenticated, logged-in download. A password-protected archive with the password sent by a separate channel also works. This confirms control of the account at the point of disclosure without adding friction now.
  3. **Escalation path.** If any red flag appears, move to Tier 2. Send a confirmation link or code to the registered email, or ask her to confirm from inside the logged-in app. Keep the search running in parallel; do not treat the clock as paused.

## 5. Search plan

Fill this from your RoPA. **Do not delete or amend anything while this runs.** Use this identifier set everywhere:
- mariela.sousa@example.com, plus any previous emails or aliases
- user ID 48213
- the billing customer ID `[CONFIRM]`
- CRM and support requester IDs `[CONFIRM]`
- analytics distinct_id / anonymous IDs `[CONFIRM]`
- name variants

| System / area | Identifiers | Owner | Due | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product DB: profile, settings, memberships, own project content (controller part), activity, consent records | user ID, email | `[CONFIRM: eng]` | 15 Mar | Open |
| Auth: login history, MFA method types (no secrets or hashes) | user ID, email | `[CONFIRM]` | 15 Mar | Open |
| Billing tool: invoices, payment history, card last 4 only | billing ID, email | `[CONFIRM: finance]` | 15 Mar | Open |
| Support tool: tickets incl. this one, internal notes | email, requester ID | `[CONFIRM: support]` | 15 Mar | Open |
| CRM / marketing: contact record, notes, campaign engagement, opt-outs | email, CRM ID | `[CONFIRM]` | 15 Mar | Open |
| Product analytics / session recordings | distinct_id, user ID | `[CONFIRM: product]` | 17 Mar | Open |
| App, audit and error logs within retention window | user ID, linkable IPs | `[CONFIRM: eng]` | 17 Mar | Open |
| Data warehouse copies, segments, scores | user ID, email | `[CONFIRM]` | 17 Mar | Open |
| Internal comms (Slack/Teams, email, docs, issue tracker) | name, email | `[CONFIRM]` | 17 Mar | Open |
| AI features, if any: prompt and response logs | user ID | `[CONFIRM]` | 17 Mar | Open / N/A |
| Backups: document what exists and its expiry | – | `[CONFIRM]` | 17 Mar | Open |
| Sub-processor assistance requests (where self-serve export isn't possible) | as above | compliance | **send by 8 Mar, due 19 Mar** | Open |
| Customer workspace content (processor part) | – | compliance | forward on confirmation | `[CONFIRM]` |

As you search, capture **named recipients** for Art. 15(1)(c) and **data sources** for Art. 15(1)(g). Record who searched what, when, and with which identifiers.

## 6. Redaction / withholding log

Nothing has been reviewed yet. Starting entries:

| # | Item / location | Decision | Ground | Reviewer | Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Support ticket of 3 Mar and forwarding thread | Disclose. Support agent names kept (customer-facing) | – | `[ ]` | `[ ]` |
| 2 | Credentials, password hashes, tokens | Not reproduced; state they are held | Security | `[ ]` | `[ ]` |
| 3 | Any internal comms naming colleagues | Disclose content about her; redact colleague identities where not essential | Art. 15(4) | `[ ]` | `[ ]` |

Internal opinions about her ("difficult user", etc.) are her personal data and **must be disclosed**.

## 7. Draft letters

**Acknowledgement (send today, reply on the same email thread):**

> **Subject:** Your data access and deletion request — ref. [DSAR ID]
>
> Dear Ms Sousa,
>
> Thank you for your email of 3 March 2027. We are treating it as two requests under the GDPR:
>
> 1. **Access to your personal data (Art. 15)**, ref. [DSAR ID]. We will provide a copy of the personal data we hold about you, plus information about how we use it, by **3 April 2027** at the latest.
> 2. **Deletion of your account (Art. 17)**, ref. [Erasure ID]. So that your access copy is complete, we will not delete anything until after we have sent it to you. We will then process the deletion and confirm what was deleted and anything we are legally required to keep (for example, invoices for tax purposes).
>
> We received your request from the email address registered on your account, so we do not need further identification. For security, we will send your data via a secure, time-limited link to this address.
>
> If you would also like us to stop sending you marketing emails in the meantime, just let us know and we will do so straight away.
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name], [Role]
> [Company legal name, address]

**Main response:** use `references/response-letter-template.md`. Fill all of headings 1–11 specifically for her:
- purposes with legal bases
- categories
- named recipients
- retention per data type
- rights, with a reference to the erasure ticket
- complaint right and your lead authority
- sources
- automated decision-making
- transfers and safeguards
- information not provided

Enclose JSON/CSV exports, a PDF summary and a README explaining the fields. Do not paste the generic privacy notice. Do not fill retention, recipients or transfer safeguards until confirmed.

## 8. Open items

- `[CONFIRM: year of receipt; deadline above assumes 2027]`
- `[CONFIRM: supervisory authority practice on Saturday / public-holiday deadlines]`
- `[CONFIRM: is she a member of any B2B customer workspace? If so, forward that part to the customer per the DPA]`
- `[CONFIRM: any red flags on the account in the last 30 days]`
- `[CONFIRM: system inventory / RoPA, sub-processor list, retention schedule]`
- `[CONFIRM: billing, CRM, support and analytics IDs for the identifier set]`
- `[CONFIRM: owner of the erasure ticket, and that deletion is on hold until access is delivered]`
- `[CONFIRM: lead supervisory authority and DPO contact for the letter]`
- `[CONFIRM: retention period for DSAR records]`

**Escalate to the DPO/counsel** if any of these arise:
- a dispute or legal context with her
- an account-takeover concern
- special-category data turns up
- you plan to withhold a whole category of documents or extend the deadline

# DSAR walkthrough: invited member of Brightwell Logistics GmbH workspace

**Questions to answer first** (placeholders are used below until you do):
1. On what date did the email reach anyone in the company?
2. Does the sender's email match a registered user account? If so, what is the user ID?
3. Which DPA clause covers data subject requests? Does it set a forwarding deadline (e.g. "without undue delay" or "within X business days")? Does it restrict what we may say to the data subject?
4. Do our terms or privacy notice treat invited members' account and login data, and our own security and telemetry, as **controller** data?
5. Who is Brightwell's privacy contact or DPO, and who is the workspace admin?

---

## 1. DSAR log entry

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| DSAR ID | `[DSAR-YYYY-NNN]` |
| Received | `[CONFIRM: date email first reached the company]` via email |
| Requester | `[name]`, `[email]`, `[CONFIRM: user ID if account exists]` |
| Relationship | Claims to be an invited member of Brightwell Logistics GmbH's workspace |
| Rights requested | Access (Art. 15) only. No erasure, rectification, portability or objection detected. |
| Role | **Processor** for workspace content (tasks, comments, in-workspace activity logs). **Possibly controller** for her user account, authentication, platform security logs and product analytics, depending on Q4. |
| Identity | Pending (see section 4) |
| Due | Controller part: `[received date + 1 month]`. Processor part: forward to Brightwell immediately. |
| Owner | `[compliance officer]` |

## 2. Scope and role decision

**The controller-vs-processor check, applied item by item:**

| Data she asked for | Who decides purposes and means? | Our role | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tasks she created in Brightwell's workspace | Brightwell. It's their workspace, used on their instructions. | Processor (per DPA) | Forward to Brightwell. Do not disclose content. |
| Comments she wrote | Brightwell | Processor | Forward to Brightwell |
| Activity log / audit trail shown inside the workspace (who edited what) | Brightwell. It's a feature they use to administer their workspace. | Processor | Forward to Brightwell |
| Her user account (name, email, login history, MFA metadata) | Usually us, for account management and security. Check Q4. | `[CONFIRM: controller?]` | If controller, answer it ourselves under Art. 15 |
| Platform security, app and error logs; product analytics keyed to her user ID | Us, for our own purposes | Controller (typically) | Answer ourselves |
| Support tickets she raised with us directly | Us | Controller | Answer ourselves |

**Conclusion:** The core of her request (tasks, comments, workspace activity) is **processor data**. We must not answer it substantively. Brightwell is the controller and decides whether and how to respond.

Her wording, "activity logs she created", most naturally means the workspace activity feed. It may also reach our own logs, which we hold as controller. The most likely outcome is therefore a **mixed request**: forward the workspace part and handle any controller part ourselves. If, after checking Q4, we hold no controller data on her beyond what sits inside the workspace, the whole request is a forward.

**Bundled rights:** none identified. If she later asks for deletion or correction of workspace content, that also goes to Brightwell.

**Escalation flag:** Brightwell is a logistics company, so she is quite possibly an employee or contractor. If anything suggests an employment dispute or pre-action disclosure, escalate to the DPO. Do not comment on the substance to either party.

## 3. Deadline

- **Processor part:** Brightwell's one-month clock as controller. When it starts is debatable: when Brightwell receives the request, or when we, as their processor, did. Take the conservative view and treat it as running from **our** receipt date. That is why we forward the same day, or within the DPA's deadline if shorter, and give Brightwell the received date.
- **Controller part (if any):** one month from receipt, due `[received date + 1 month; if that date doesn't exist, the last day of the month]`. Internal milestones: search complete T-14, draft T-7, sign-off T-3.
- **Extension:** not anticipated. The controller-side volume is small.

## 4. Identity decision

- **Processor part:** verification is Brightwell's job as controller. We should not ask her for ID for this part. We would also have nothing to verify on Brightwell's behalf.
- **Controller part:**
  - If her email matches the registered account email, that is Tier 1 and no further ID is needed.
  - If the email doesn't match, or we can't find an account, it is Tier 2. Send a confirmation link or code to the registered email, or ask her to resubmit while logged in. Don't ask for passport copies.
- **Red flag check:** look for a recent email change, password reset or new device on the account. Also check whether she asks for delivery to a different address. Any of these moves her up a tier.
- **Holding reply:** keep it neutral. It should not confirm that an account exists or that we hold data, because she isn't verified yet.

## 5. Search plan (controller part only)

| System | Identifiers | Owner | Due | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Users/auth tables (account, login history, MFA metadata; no secrets or hashes) | email, user ID | Eng | T-14 | Open |
| Security/app logs, Sentry, within retention window | user ID, IPs linked to her sessions | Eng | T-14 | Open |
| Product analytics (e.g. distinct_id) | user ID, anonymous IDs merged on login | Product | T-14 | Open |
| Support tool (tickets she raised with *us*) | email | Support | T-14 | Open |
| CRM/marketing (if she was ever a lead or on lists) | email | Sales/Marketing | T-14 | Open |
| Workspace tasks/comments/activity | n/a | Do not search for disclosure. Only assist Brightwell if instructed. | Per Brightwell's instruction | Forwarded |

**Rule for all systems:** don't delete or amend anything in either part because the request arrived. Record who searched what, when, and with which identifiers.

## 6. Redaction/withholding log

| # | Item | Decision | Ground |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Workspace tasks, comments and activity logs | Not disclosed by us | Processor data. Request forwarded to the controller (Brightwell) under Art. 28(3)(e) and the DPA. This is not a redaction ground; we are simply not the right party to answer. |
| 2 | Credentials, hashes, tokens (controller part) | Not reproduced | Security. State that they are held. |

## 7. Draft letters

### A. Holding reply to the requester

This reply does not disclose workspace content or confirm what we hold. It does not promise anything on Brightwell's behalf and doesn't speak for them.

> **Subject:** Your request for access to personal data – ref. [DSAR ID]
>
> Dear [name],
>
> Thank you for your message, which we received on [date].
>
> You have asked for personal data contained in tasks, comments and activity logs within the Brightwell Logistics GmbH workspace on our platform. For content in that workspace, we act as a service provider (processor) on behalf of Brightwell Logistics GmbH, which is the controller responsible for that data under the GDPR. This means Brightwell Logistics GmbH decides how requests about that content are handled. We have passed your request to them [today / on [date]], and we will assist them in responding. You may also contact them directly: [Brightwell privacy contact, if known, otherwise: "for example via your workspace administrator or their privacy team"].
>
> Separately, we may hold limited personal data about you for our own purposes, for example to operate user accounts and keep the platform secure. We will handle that part of your request ourselves. [If verification needed: To protect your data, please confirm this request by [clicking the link we have sent to the email address registered on the account / submitting it while logged in].] We will respond on that part by [due date].
>
> Please quote [DSAR ID] in any reply.
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name, role]
> [Company legal name, address]

**Before sending, check the DPA.** If it prohibits *any* communication with data subjects without Brightwell's instruction, send Brightwell the forward first. Then send only the minimal redirect, which is the first paragraph without our role explanation, or follow whatever Brightwell instructs. Most DPAs allow this redirect, but verify.

### B. Forwarding notice to Brightwell (yes, you must notify them)

Notification is required. Art. 28(3)(e) obliges us to assist the controller with data subject requests, and the DPA almost certainly requires prompt forwarding. Brightwell's own one-month clock is likely already running, so forward immediately.

> **To:** [Brightwell privacy contact / DPO / workspace admin]
> **Subject:** Data subject access request concerning your workspace – our ref. [DSAR ID]
>
> Dear [name],
>
> Under clause [x] of our Data Processing Agreement, we are forwarding a data subject request we received on [date] from [requester name, email], who states she is an invited member of your workspace. She asks for a copy of the personal data in tasks, comments and activity logs she created. A copy of her request is attached.
>
> As controller, Brightwell Logistics GmbH is responsible for responding to her about that content. We have not disclosed any workspace data to her. We have told her that we have passed her request to you.
>
> Workspace admins can export this data via [admin export feature / path]. If you need our assistance, for example a targeted export by user, please instruct us in writing and we will provide it by [date]. Please note the request was received on [date], which may be relevant to your response deadline.
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name, role]

## 8. Open items

- `[CONFIRM: exact date the request first reached the company]`
- `[CONFIRM: does the sender's email match a registered account? user ID?]`
- `[CONFIRM: DPA clause number, forwarding deadline, and any limits on communicating with data subjects]`
- `[CONFIRM: are invited members' account, auth, security-log and analytics data controller data under our terms/RoPA?]`
- `[CONFIRM: Brightwell privacy/DPO contact and workspace admin]`
- `[CONFIRM: whether an admin export tool exists that Brightwell can use]`
- **Escalate to DPO** if Brightwell refuses or fails to respond, if signs of an employment dispute or litigation appear, or if the account shows takeover red flags.
- Log every date: received, forwarded to Brightwell, holding reply sent, verification, controller-part response.

*This is a working draft for your review, not legal advice. Confirm the role classification and DPA wording with your DPO or counsel before sending.*

# DSAR response pack: Tomasz Nowak (ex-employee, now customer)

## Questions to answer first

1. **Request details.** What is the exact wording, channel and date received by anyone in the company? The extension notice must reach him within one month of that date. If that month has already passed, you cannot extend and the response is late.
2. **Scope.** Did he ask for "all data", or only his customer data? If he asked for everything, his **employee-era data (HR, payroll, staff email, his own Slack activity) is in scope** and has not been searched yet.
3. **Dispute.** Is there any dispute, employment claim or complaint involving him? The legal advice in Slack suggests there may be.
4. **Fraud model.** Was the fraud-scoring model actually applied to him? If so, what score or flag did he get, and did it lead to any decision (block, review, limit) without human involvement?
5. **Zendesk tickets.** Are the tickets with other customers' staff names tickets **he raised as a customer**, or tickets **he handled as an employee**?
6. **Company details.** I need your legal name, lead supervisory authority, DPO contact, sub-processor list, hosting provider and region, and retention schedule.

---

## 1. DSAR log entry

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| DSAR ID | [CONFIRM: DSAR ID] |
| Received | [CONFIRM: date received by anyone in company] via [CONFIRM: channel] |
| Requester | Tomasz Nowak, [CONFIRM: email(s)], customer ID [CONFIRM], Stripe `cus_` [CONFIRM], former employee ID [CONFIRM] |
| Relationship | Former employee, now customer |
| Representative | [CONFIRM: none / name + written authority] |
| Rights requested | Access (Art. 15). [CONFIRM: any erasure, rectification, objection or marketing opt-out? Log each separately] |
| Role | Controller for all categories identified (customer account, billing, CRM, support, logs, HR) [CONFIRM: no B2B customer workspace content involved] |
| Identity | Tier 3 (ex-employee / HR data). See §4 |
| Due (base) | [CONFIRM: received date + 1 calendar month] |
| Extension | Proposed, up to 2 months, to [CONFIRM: received date + 3 months]. Reasons must be specific; see §3 |
| Escalated to DPO/counsel | **Yes, required.** Triggers: ex-employee/HR data, legal privilege, fraud/security material, trade-secret claim on decision logic, possible dispute |
| Approver | [CONFIRM: name] |

---

## 2. Scope and role decision

- **Controller.** You are controller for everything gathered so far: product DB, Zendesk, HubSpot, Stripe and server logs. If he asked for "all data", you are also controller for his former employment records. No processor-forwarding is needed unless his account sits inside a B2B customer's workspace [CONFIRM].
- **Ex-employee status.** This widens scope and raises risk. The skill requires counsel review for HR DSARs. Employee-era material includes appraisals, disciplinary notes, exit documents and messages about him. It is often what the requester actually wants, especially before a claim.
- **Bundled rights.** None identified in what you sent [CONFIRM against the verbatim request].
- **Do not delete or amend anything** because of the request. The response reflects data held on the date received.

---

## 3. Deadline and extension decision

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Received | [CONFIRM] |
| Base due date | [CONFIRM: same date next month; last day of month if that date doesn't exist; verify weekend/holiday handling with your authority] |
| Extension notice must be sent by | The base due date at the latest. Send it now |
| Extended due date | Up to [CONFIRM: received + 3 months]. Aim earlier; the limit is a backstop |

**Should you extend? Yes, but "volume" alone is a weak reason as written.**

Art. 12(3) allows an extension only "where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests". Supervisory authorities reject backlog, staff holidays or poor data mapping. You have already gathered five systems, which undercuts a pure volume argument. The defensible reasons here are about complexity:

- Employee-era records across HR, payroll, staff email and internal messaging still need to be searched (if in scope).
- Material needs review by external counsel for legal privilege.
- Multiple third parties appear in support records and require individual balancing.
- Fraud and security material requires specialist review.

Put the specific reasons in the notice and keep evidence of them in the file. **Send what is ready with the notice.** The Stripe billing records and product DB profile are good candidates.

## 6. Redaction / withholding log

### A. Other customers' staff names in Zendesk tickets: redact narrowly (Art. 15(4), Recital 63)

Apply the decision steps ticket by ticket:

1. **Is the third party identifiable?** If not, there is nothing to redact.
2. **Did Tomasz already know the information?** If he wrote or received the message as a customer, the names are usually already known to him. Disclose, unless the item includes private details such as personal contact data.
3. **Are these tickets he handled as an employee?** Then the ticket content is mainly other customers' personal data, not his. Disclose the parts that relate to him: his name as agent, his actions, his replies, and any internal notes or ratings about his handling. Redact the other customers' identities and unrelated content.
4. **Would disclosure harm the third party?** This covers complaints about him or personal details. If so, redact the identifying parts and keep the content about Tomasz.
5. **Our own support agents' names:** customer-facing, so keep them.

Use proper redaction in the source export. Do not draw black boxes over a PDF, and strip metadata.

### B. Slack notes containing external counsel's legal advice: withhold only the advice, and only once counsel confirms

- Legal privilege is **not in the GDPR text**. It applies only through member-state law under Art. 23. **Do not self-certify.** External counsel must confirm that the passages are privileged under [CONFIRM: member state] law and record the provision relied on.
- **Withhold only the privileged communications.** Surrounding Slack messages about Tomasz that are not legal advice must be disclosed. This includes colleagues' opinions and comments such as "difficult customer", because opinions about him are his personal data (CJEU C-434/16 *Nowak*). Redact colleagues' names where not essential, and their unrelated chatter.
- The response letter should say that some material was withheld on the ground of legal professional privilege, in general terms, without revealing the advice.
- The existence of legal advice about him suggests a dispute or pre-action context. That makes **DPO/counsel escalation mandatory** for the whole response.

### C. Fraud-scoring model: disclose his data and meaningful logic; withhold only what enables circumvention or is a genuine trade secret

- **The model description document itself** (architecture, features, weights, thresholds) is generally not his personal data. You do not need to disclose it as such.
- **What he must receive if the model was applied to him:**
  - His score, flag or outcome.
  - The personal data used as inputs.
  - Any decision taken and when.
  - Who reviewed it, if anyone. Staff identities are in principle not required (CJEU C-579/21).
- **If the decision was solely automated with legal or similarly significant effects** (e.g. account blocked or payment refused), Art. 15(1)(h) requires meaningful information about:
  - the logic involved,
  - its significance, and
  - the envisaged consequences.
- **Trade-secret claim.** A trade secret is not a blanket refusal ground. Recital 63 says the result must not be a refusal to provide all information. CJEU C-203/22 (*Dun & Bradstreet Austria*) indicates that where you claim trade secrets, the information may need to go to the supervisory authority or court to balance. Verify the current position with counsel.
- **Security ground.** Detection rules and thresholds whose disclosure would let fraudsters evade the model can be withheld under Art. 15(4) or a national Art. 23 restriction [CONFIRM: national provision verified by counsel].
- **Engineering's label of "trade secret" is not enough on its own.** Log the specific items withheld and why.

### D. Other items (not raised, but they apply)

- **HubSpot notes:** disclose opinions and assessments in full. Embarrassing comments are not a redaction ground.
- **Stripe:** payment method shown as brand and last 4 digits only. Never the full card number.
- **Product DB and auth:** do not reproduce password hashes, MFA secrets, API keys or session tokens. State that they are held but not reproduced.
- **Server logs:** include only IPs and records you can link to him. Exclude shared or NAT traffic you cannot attribute.
